requirements.requirement: Run a containerized web application as the unprivileged appsvc account (no root involvement in serving process)
requirements.summary: appsvc (uid 1001) was created and, per post-reboot process listing, every relevant process (rootlesskit, dockerd, containerd, docker-proxy, nginx master) runs under uid 1001 with no root involvement. This was confirmed after a full reboot, not just at initial setup.

curl to NODE_IP:8080 returned HTTP 200 with nginx content before the reboot cycle, and again after each of two reboots; ss/rootlesskit shows the real listener on :::8080 mapped via rootlesskit's port-forwarding API to the container's port 80.

requirements.requirement: Application starts at boot while appsvc has no active login session
requirements.summary: Lingering was enabled for appsvc (loginctl enable-linger); loginctl list-sessions confirms no session existed for appsvc both before and after reboot, while appsvc's systemd --user docker.service, the boot-time cgroup-delegation unit, and the webapp container all came up automatically after node1 was rebooted (systemctl reboot), producing a changed boot_id and a fully automatic HTTP 200 response. A genuine bounded-disruption/recovery cycle was captured, including a first-reboot failure (cgroup ownership reset) that was root-caused and fixed, then re-verified end-to-end on a second reboot.

overall_summary: All three material outcomes of the task — a containerized web app running entirely as unprivileged appsvc, serving on port 8080, and starting automatically at boot with no active appsvc login session — are directly and coherently supported by evidence, including two full reboot cycles that captured a genuine baseline/disruption/recovery transition (the first reboot even exposed and required fixing a real cgroup-delegation gap, which was then re-verified end-to-end on a second reboot). Hygiene is generally good given the extreme platform constraints (32-bit Ubuntu 16.04, kernel 4.4, no native rootless tooling), with two minor retained loose-ends: a permission widening on /etc/docker/key.json and an unnecessary systemd-journal group grant for appsvc.
limitations: Long compile/build troubleshooting sequences (meson/ninja/python version mismatches) are read-only diagnostics or corrective retries and were not counted as unnecessary mutations, though the trace does not exhaustively confirm every intermediate build artifact was cleaned up.

The provider-wide restart-evidence protocol overlaps completely with the task's own boot-behavior requirement here, so no additional restart evidence gap exists beyond what was already assessed against the task contract.

operational_hygiene.summary: The bulk of the executor's actions (compiling rootlesskit/slirp4netns/ninja/libslirp, installing dockerd-rootless scripts, configuring cgroup delegation and the rootlesskit port-registration ExecStartPost) were necessary, evidence-backed workarounds for a 32-bit Ubuntu 16.04/kernel 4.4 host lacking native rootless-container support, and none were left in a broken or conflicting state — the final systemd units (docker.service, appsvc-cgroup-delegate.service) were both active with no failed units at after_executor (global:after_executor:node1:failed-services empty). Two items lower the score: (1) cmd-30e187efe907451a widened /etc/docker/key.json from 600 to 644 (world-readable) to work around a rootless permission error, and this looser permission was never reverted — a retained, low-severity weakening of a root-owned file's protection. (2) cmd-5d7b90d1f5f94673 added appsvc to the systemd-journal group purely for troubleshooting journal visibility; this grant was not needed for the final working solution and was left in place. Both are bounded and low-risk (not destructive, not broadly scoped) but were retained beyond their diagnostic purpose.
